abstract.text: Aspects of scientific method are discussed: In particular, its representation as a motivated iteration in which, in succession, practice confronts theory, and theory, practice. Rapid progress requires sufficient flexibility to profit from such confrontations, and the ability to devise parsimonious but effective models, to worry selectively about model inadequacies and to employ mathematics skillfully but appropriately. The development of statistical methods at Rothamsted Experimental Station by Sir Ronald Fisher is used to illustrate these themes.

thesis.text: Scientific and statistical progress depends on a motivated, flexible iteration between theory and practice, requiring parsimony, selective attention, appropriate mathematics, and closed-loop feedback; Fisher's Rothamsted work exemplifies this method.

The extraordinary extent to which Fisher's actual every day experience was grist to the mill of his inductive mind is further illustrated in the famous opening lines of Chapter II of Fisher's book The Design of Experiments [11, p. 11]
This resulted in Fisher's pioneering work on nonlinear design in 1922 mentioned by Cochran [4].
In cooperation with Fisher the problem was tackled rather differently. The authors note [14, p. 180]
This work was published in a series of papers having the general title "Studies in Crop Variation" and numbered r, II, III,2 IV, and VI [7, 13, 8, 5, 6].

In "Studies in Crop Variation I" [7], Fisher begins by presenting a workmanlike discussion, which lasts for twelve pages, of the responses to the thirteen different manures revealed by his analysis of the Broadbalk data.
says [7, p. 123] "it is a weakness of the polynomial form that the extreme terms should be so much affected."
He speculates [7, p. 129], "Of all the organic factors which influence the yield of wheat it is probable that weeds alone change sufficiently slowly to explain the changes at Broadbalk."
But he says [7, p. 131] "it may be remembered that the Education Acts of 1876 and 1880 made attendance at school compulsory."
Indeed, much can still be learnt from his discussion about economical processes of calculation and appropriate checks [8, p. 111-3].

In "Studies in Crop Variation II," jointly authored with his assistant, Miss W.A. MacKenzie, and subtitled "The Manurial Response of Different Potato Varieties," [13] he tried his hand at analyzing some experimental data from Rothamsted.
form of the appropriate correction came quickly in the first edition of Statistical Methods in 1925 (see [12, p. 238]).

After the algebraic identity between the total suin of squares and the within and between treatments suni of squares has been written down, the statement is made [13, p. 315] "If all the plots were undifferentiated, as if the numbers had been mixed up and written down in random order, the average value of each of the two parts is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom in the variation of which it is compared."

The authors say [13, p. 316], "the above test is only given as an illustration of the method; the summation formula for combining the effects of variety and manurial treatment is evidently quite unsuitable for the purpose."

With the possibility of transformation so much a part of Fisher's everyday thought, we might expect him now to proceed along that route but in fact he derives the appropriate nonlinear analysis, devising methods which have only recently been rediscovered [18].
When Fisher's friend Gosset saw the paper, he wrote to Fisher [15, Letter No. 29], "The experiment seems to me to be quite badly planned, you should give them a hand in that....."
Fisher later notes Gosset's "suggesting that I should start designing experiments" [15, summary of Letter No. 29].
But between 1924 and 1929, as described in "Studies in Crop Variation IV and VI" [5, 6], there is a rapid development of ideas which were quickly put into practice.

In spite of all this in 1926 the Director of Rothamsted, Sir John Russell, wrote a paper [16] in the Journal of the Ministry of Agriculture about agricultural experimentation which almost totally ignored the ideas of his proteg6.
However, in the next issue [9] in a paper notable for its brevity and clarity, Fisher outlined his philosophy on the subject, setting his boss to rights and anyone else who would listen.
I have cited already the development of distribution-free tests which, he felt, misused ideas initiated in Chapter III of his book Design of Experiments [11, p. 48].
As long ago as 1950, Fisher, delivering the Eddington Memorial Lecture at Cambridge, said [10, p. 22]

To quote Fisher once more, in 1952, in a letter concerning a proposed Statistics Center to be set up in Scotland he said: "I have no hesitation in advising that such a centre as you have under discussion should plan to integrate teaching closely with project work in which practical experience can be gained by those who are capable of learning from it; in contradistinction to the ruinous process of segregating the keener minds into a completely sterile atmosphere" [3].

relations.why: Box uses Fisher's letter to support his argument that statisticians should be trained through project work rather than sterile theory alone.

sections.summary: Box argues that science advances by motivated iteration between theory and practice, requiring flexibility, parsimony, selective worry, and appropriately used mathematics. Fisher is introduced as a practical scientist whose everyday experiences—Rothamsted, baby weights, tea tasting, bacterial counts, and extreme values—feed his inductive, iterative style.
sections.title: Theory-Practice Iteration and Fisher's Scientific Method

source_span.end_text: "The analysis of variance, hinted at earlier, appears here for the first time in its completeness."
source_span.start_text: "In the inferential stage, the analyst acts as a sponsor for the model."

sections.summary: Fisher's crop-variation papers illustrate data analysis as iteration: Broadbalk manure data lead to orthogonal polynomials and residual checks; rainfall-wheat modeling leads to distributed lags and transfer functions; potato fertilizer data lead to ANOVA and nonlinear interaction. Residual analysis and parsimonious modeling are shown as integral to scientific inference.
sections.title: Rothamsted Case Studies in Iterative Statistics

source_span.end_text: "It is surely because he was all of these that he was much more than the sum of the parts."
source_span.start_text: "This was one important reason for Fisher's insistence (i) on the physical act of randomization as a necessary condition for the validity of any experiment"

sections.summary: Fisher's field experience makes randomization essential for valid inference; distribution-free tests do not remove dependence unless randomization is used. His designs evolve through replication, blocking, factorial arrangements, and confounding. Open-loop statistics stagnates in cookbookery or mathematistry, so the remedy is training scientist-statisticians who balance theory and practice.
sections.title: Randomization, Design, and the Statistician's Role

relations.quote: The extraordinary extent to which Fisher's actual every day experience was grist to the mill of his inductive mind is further illustrated in the famous opening lines of Chapter II of Fisher's book The Design of Experiments [11, p. 11]
relations.why: The Design of Experiments supplies the tea-tasting example and later the distribution-free-test idea that Box uses and critiques.

relations.quote: When Fisher's friend Gosset saw the paper, he wrote to Fisher [15, Letter No. 29], "The experiment seems to me to be quite badly planned, you should give them a hand in that....."
relations.why: Gosset's letter illustrates the feedback from critiquing an analysis to designing future experiments.

relations.quote: In spite of all this in 1926 the Director of Rothamsted, Sir John Russell, wrote a paper [16] in the Journal of the Ministry of Agriculture about agricultural experimentation which almost totally ignored the ideas of his proteg6.
relations.why: Russell's paper is the counterexample: established practice ignored Fisher's iterative design ideas until Fisher replied.

relations.quote: To quote Fisher once more, in 1952, in a letter concerning a proposed Statistics Center to be set up in Scotland he said: "I have no hesitation in advising that such a centre as you have under discussion should plan to integrate teaching closely with project work in which practical experience can be gained by those who are capable of learning from it; in contradistinction to the ruinous process of segregating the keener minds into a completely sterile atmosphere" [3].
relations.why: Box uses Fisher's letter to support his argument that statisticians should be trained through project work rather than sterile theory alone.

source_span.end_text: "The next leg of the scientific iteration is hinted at as he goes on to discuss how best to plot the data so as to make \"a rough examination of the agreement of observation with any (proposed) law of increase.\""
source_span.start_text: "Aspects of scientific method are discussed: In particular, its representation as a motivated iteration in which, in succession, practice confronts theory, and theory, practice."

sections.summary: Box argues that science advances by motivated iteration between theory and practice, requiring flexibility, parsimony, selective worry, and appropriately used mathematics. Fisher is introduced as a practical scientist whose everyday experiences—Rothamsted, baby weights, tea tasting, bacterial counts, and extreme values—feed his inductive, iterative style.
sections.title: Theory-Practice Iteration and Fisher's Scientific Method

source_span.end_text: "The analysis of variance, hinted at earlier, appears here for the first time in its completeness."
source_span.start_text: "In the inferential stage, the analyst acts as a sponsor for the model."

sections.summary: Fisher's crop-variation papers illustrate data analysis as iteration: Broadbalk manure data lead to orthogonal polynomials and residual checks; rainfall-wheat modeling leads to distributed lags and transfer functions; potato fertilizer data lead to ANOVA and nonlinear interaction. Residual analysis and parsimonious modeling are shown as integral to scientific inference.
sections.title: Rothamsted Case Studies in Iterative Statistics

source_span.end_text: "It is surely because he was all of these that he was much more than the sum of the parts."
source_span.start_text: "This was one important reason for Fisher's insistence (i) on the physical act of randomization as a necessary condition for the validity of any experiment"

sections.summary: Fisher's field experience makes randomization essential for valid inference; distribution-free tests do not remove dependence unless randomization is used. His designs evolve through replication, blocking, factorial arrangements, and confounding. Open-loop statistics stagnates in cookbookery or mathematistry, so the remedy is training scientist-statisticians who balance theory and practice.
sections.title: Randomization, Design, and the Statistician's Role
